decks.title: Colligative Properties — Part 1: Vapour pressure, boiling point and freezing point
goals: Explain why colligative properties depend on the number, not the nature, of solute particles
Calculate molar mass from the relative lowering of vapour pressure
Derive the expressions for elevation of boiling point and depression of freezing point
Calculate molar mass from boiling point elevation and freezing point depression

slides.heading: Colligative properties
slides.body_md: Part 1 — three effects of a non-volatile solute that depend only on **how many** particles it supplies.

visual.alt: Flow: adding a non-volatile solute causes four colligative effects

slides.narration: Why is salt spread on icy roads in cold countries, why does a pressure cooker of salted water take a little longer to boil, and how did chemists find the molar mass of new compounds before modern instruments? All of these involve colligative properties: properties of a solution that depend only on the number of solute particles, not on what they are. In this part we meet three of them and derive their equations.

slides.heading: What “colligative” means
slides.body_md: Colligative means “bound together”: all four effects depend on the **number of solute particles per amount of solvent**. One mole of glucose and one mole of urea in the same mass of water give the same effects; one mole of NaCl, which gives two moles of ions, gives about twice the effect.

visual.alt: Table comparing the number of particles and relative colligative effect of four solutes

slides.narration: The word colligative means bound together. All four effects are tied to one quantity: how many solute particles are dissolved in a given amount of solvent. A mole of glucose and a mole of urea act exactly alike. But a mole of potassium chloride splits into two moles of ions and gives about twice the effect. Keep this particle-counting idea in mind throughout the chapter.

slides.heading: Lowering of vapour pressure
slides.body_md: Solute particles occupy part of the surface, so **fewer solvent molecules escape** per second: the vapour pressure of a solution of a non-volatile solute is lower than that of the pure solvent.

visual.alt: Pure solvent with many particles escaping from the surface beside a solution in which solute particles occupy part of the surface and fewer solvent particles escape
visual.caption: Schematic: fewer solvent particles at the surface means fewer escape per second.

slides.narration: At the surface of a pure solvent every spot is a solvent molecule that could escape. In a solution, some surface spots are taken by solute particles that cannot evaporate, so fewer solvent molecules escape each second and the vapour pressure is lower. The more solute particles, the larger the lowering.

slides.heading: Relative lowering of vapour pressure
slides.body_md: From Raoult’s law, $p = p^\circ x_1$, so the **relative lowering** of vapour pressure equals the **mole fraction of the solute**. For a dilute solution, $n_2 \ll n_1$, which gives the molar mass $M_2$ of the solute.

rows: Vapour pressure of pure solvent, of solution
Mass and molar mass of solvent
Mass and molar mass of solute

visual.alt: Table of symbols in the relative lowering equation

slides.narration: Raoult’s law gives a neat result: the lowering of vapour pressure divided by the pure solvent’s vapour pressure equals the mole fraction of the solute. This is the relative lowering, and it depends only on how many solute particles there are. In a dilute solution we can write it in terms of masses and molar masses, and solve for the unknown molar mass of the solute.

slides.heading: Worked example: molar mass from vapour pressure lowering
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** $2.0\ \text{g}$ of a non-volatile solute is dissolved in $39\ \text{g}$ of benzene ($M = 78$). The vapour pressure falls from $10.00\ \text{kPa}$ to $9.80\ \text{kPa}$. Find the molar mass of the solute.

**Step 1.** Relative lowering $= (10.00 - 9.80) \div 10.00 = 0.020$.

**Step 2.** $0.020 = \dfrac{w_2 M_1}{M_2 w_1} = \dfrac{2.0 \times 78}{M_2 \times 39}$.

**Step 3.** $M_2 = \dfrac{156}{0.020 \times 39} = \dfrac{156}{0.78} = 200\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Table of the steps in the molar mass calculation from vapour pressure lowering

slides.narration: First find the relative lowering: a drop of nought point two kilopascal out of ten is two hundredths. Set this equal to the solute mass times the solvent molar mass, divided by the solute molar mass times the solvent mass. Rearranging, the molar mass is one hundred and fifty six divided by nought point seven eight, which is two hundred grams per mole.

slides.heading: Why a solution boils at a higher temperature
slides.body_md: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure. The solution’s vapour pressure curve lies **below** the solvent’s, so it must be heated more: $\Delta T_\text{b} = T_\text{b} - T^\circ_\text{b}$.

visual.alt: Vapour pressure against temperature near the boiling point: the solution curve runs just below and nearly parallel to the pure-solvent curve, so it reaches atmospheric pressure at a higher temperature; the gap between the two boiling points is the elevation
visual.caption: Illustrative; over this small range the curves are nearly straight and parallel, which is the basis of the derivation.

slides.narration: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure reaches the pressure of the atmosphere. The solution’s curve always lies a little below the pure solvent’s curve, because the solute lowers the vapour pressure. So the solution reaches atmospheric pressure only at a higher temperature. Near the boiling point the two curves are almost straight and parallel, which we use in the derivation.

slides.heading: Derivation: elevation of boiling point
slides.body_md: Near $T^\circ_\text{b}$ the two curves are almost parallel straight lines, so the elevation is proportional to the lowering of vapour pressure, $\Delta T_\text{b} \propto \Delta p$. Since $p^\circ$ (equal to atmospheric pressure at $T^\circ_\text{b}$) is constant, $\Delta T_\text{b} \propto \Delta p / p^\circ = x_2$. For a dilute solution $x_2 \approx n_2/n_1$, and $n_2/n_1 = m M_1/1000$, where $m$ is the molality. So $\Delta T_\text{b} = K m$ with $K$ a constant for the solvent, the **ebullioscopic constant** $K_\text{b}$.

visual.alt: Table of ebullioscopic and cryoscopic constants for common solvents

math: \Delta T_\text{b} = K_\text{b}\, m = \frac{1000\, K_\text{b}\, w_2}{M_2\, w_1}
slides.narration: Here is the derivation. Close to the boiling point the vapour pressure curves of the solvent and the solution are nearly straight and parallel, so the rise in boiling point is proportional to the lowering of vapour pressure. That lowering, divided by the constant pure vapour pressure, is the mole fraction of solute, which for a dilute solution is proportional to the molality. So the elevation equals a constant times the molality.

slides.heading: Worked example: molar mass from boiling point elevation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A solution of $1.8\ \text{g}$ of a non-volatile solute in $60\ \text{g}$ of water boils at $373.28\ \text{K}$ (pure water $373.15\ \text{K}$; $K_\text{b} = 0.52\ \text{K kg mol}^{-1}$). Find the molar mass.

**Step 1.** $\Delta T_\text{b} = 373.28 - 373.15 = 0.13\ \text{K}$.

**Step 2.** $M_2 = \dfrac{1000 K_\text{b} w_2}{\Delta T_\text{b} w_1} = \dfrac{1000 \times 0.52 \times 1.8}{0.13 \times 60}$.

**Step 3.** $M_2 = \dfrac{936}{7.8} = 120\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Flow for finding molar mass from boiling point elevation

slides.narration: The boiling point rose by nought point one three kelvin. Rearrange the equation to make the molar mass the subject, keeping masses in grams so that the factor of one thousand converts grams of solvent to kilograms. The top is nine hundred and thirty six, the bottom seven point eight, and the molar mass comes out at one hundred and twenty grams per mole.

slides.heading: Why a solution freezes at a lower temperature
slides.body_md: At the freezing point, the solid and liquid have the **same vapour pressure**. The solution’s vapour pressure is lower, so its curve meets the steep solid curve at a **lower temperature**.

visual.alt: Vapour pressure against temperature near the freezing point: the steep line for the solid crosses the liquid-solvent line at the normal freezing point and crosses the lower solution line at a lower temperature, which is the freezing point of the solution
visual.caption: Illustrative curves. The solution freezes where its vapour pressure equals that of the solid solvent.

slides.narration: At the freezing point, the solid solvent and the liquid have exactly the same vapour pressure. The solid’s vapour pressure falls very steeply as it cools. Because the solution’s vapour pressure is lower than the pure liquid’s, the solid curve meets the solution curve only at a lower temperature. That lower crossing point is the freezing point of the solution.

slides.heading: Depression of freezing point
slides.body_md: By the same argument (nearly straight curves near $T^\circ_\text{f}$), $\Delta T_\text{f} = T^\circ_\text{f} - T_\text{f} \propto \Delta p \propto x_2$, and for dilute solutions $\Delta T_\text{f} = K_\text{f}\, m$. $K_\text{f}$, the **cryoscopic constant** (molal depression constant), is the depression for a $1\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$ solution. Both constants depend only on the solvent; thermodynamically $K_\text{f} = \dfrac{R (T^\circ_\text{f})^2 M_1}{1000\, \Delta_\text{fus}H}$.

headers: How the freezing point is lowered
rows: Brine freezes below 0 °C, so ice melts
Ethylene glycol keeps coolant liquid in winter
Large Kf (37.7) gives easily measured depressions

visual.alt: Table of uses of freezing point depression

math: \Delta T_\text{f} = K_\text{f}\, m = \frac{1000\, K_\text{f}\, w_2}{M_2\, w_1}
slides.narration: The same reasoning gives the depression of freezing point: it is proportional to the lowering of vapour pressure, and so to the molality, with the cryoscopic constant as the proportionality constant. Both constants depend only on the solvent. Camphor has an unusually large cryoscopic constant, so it gives large, easily measured depressions, which is useful for finding molar masses.

slides.heading: Worked example: protecting a radiator
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** What mass of ethylene glycol ($M = 62$) must be added to $2.5\ \text{kg}$ of water so that the coolant does not freeze above $-9.3\ ^\circ\text{C}$? ($K_\text{f} = 1.86\ \text{K kg mol}^{-1}$)

**Step 1.** $\Delta T_\text{f} = 9.3\ \text{K}$; $m = 9.3 \div 1.86 = 5.0\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$.

**Step 2.** Moles $= 5.0 \times 2.5 = 12.5\ \text{mol}$.

**Step 3.** Mass $= 12.5 \times 62 = 775\ \text{g}$.

visual.alt: Table of the steps in the antifreeze calculation

slides.narration: Work backwards from the target temperature. A freezing point of minus nine point three degrees means a depression of nine point three kelvin; a temperature difference is the same in kelvin and in degrees. Dividing by the cryoscopic constant gives a molality of five. In two and a half kilograms of water that is twelve and a half mole, or seven hundred and seventy five grams of ethylene glycol.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles, not their nature.
Relative lowering of vapour pressure $= x_2 \approx \dfrac{w_2 M_1}{M_2 w_1}$.
$\Delta T_\text{b} = K_\text{b} m$ and $\Delta T_\text{f} = K_\text{f} m$, derived from $\Delta T \propto \Delta p \propto x_2$.
$K_\text{b}$ and $K_\text{f}$ depend only on the solvent (K kg mol⁻¹).
Each property gives the molar mass of a non-volatile solute.

visual.alt: Summary table of the three colligative equations in Part 1

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. A non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of the solvent; the relative lowering equals the mole fraction of solute. As a result, the solution boils at a higher temperature and freezes at a lower one, and both changes are proportional to molality. Each of these properties can be used to find the molar mass of the solute.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: A temperature difference is the same in K and °C.
Use grams in the 1000 Kb w₂ ÷ (M₂ w₁) form; kilograms in Kb × m.
For derivations, state the assumptions: dilute solution, non-volatile solute, curves nearly parallel near Tb or Tf.
Kb and Kf depend on the solvent only.

visual.alt: Table of common traps in Part 1 and fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. A temperature difference is the same in kelvin and degrees Celsius. Be consistent with units: grams with the factor of one thousand, or kilograms with plain molality. In derivations, state the assumptions clearly. And remember the constants belong to the solvent.

slides.heading: Osmosis and abnormal molar masses
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the fourth colligative property, and what happens when solutes split up or pair up.

nodes.label: Osmotic pressure and van’t Hoff laws

visual.alt: Flow of the topics in Part 2

slides.narration: Why does a raisin swell in water, why does a cucumber shrivel in salt, and how is sea water made drinkable on ships? All involve osmosis. In this part we study osmotic pressure, which obeys laws very like the gas laws, and then we see why salts and some acids give colligative effects that are too large or too small.

slides.heading: Diffusion and osmosis
slides.body_md: **Diffusion:** spontaneous spreading of solute (and solvent) particles from higher to lower concentration until uniform; no membrane needed. **Osmosis:** net flow of **solvent only** through a **semipermeable membrane** (e.g. parchment, cellophane, copper ferrocyanide film, animal bladder) from pure solvent or a dilute solution into a more concentrated solution.

rows: Solute from high to low concentration
Solvent from dilute to concentrated solution

visual.alt: Table comparing diffusion and osmosis

slides.narration: Diffusion and osmosis are often confused. In diffusion, particles spread out on their own until the mixture is uniform; no membrane is involved, and both solute and solvent move. In osmosis, a semipermeable membrane lets only solvent molecules through, so solvent flows from the dilute side to the concentrated side. Osmosis can be stopped by applying pressure; diffusion cannot.

slides.heading: Osmotic pressure
slides.body_md: The **osmotic pressure** $\pi$ of a solution is the excess pressure that must be applied to the solution to just prevent the flow of pure solvent into it through a semipermeable membrane.

slides.heading: van’t Hoff laws of osmotic pressure
slides.body_md: van’t Hoff found that dilute solutions behave like gases. **Boyle–van’t Hoff law:** at constant $T$, $\pi \propto C$. **Charles–van’t Hoff law:** at constant $C$, $\pi \propto T$. **Avogadro–van’t Hoff law:** equimolar solutions at the same temperature have equal osmotic pressures. Combining them, $\pi = CRT$, i.e. $\pi V = nRT$, with $R$ the gas constant.

rows: Equal π for equimolar solutions at the same T

visual.alt: Table of the three van’t Hoff laws for osmotic pressure with their gas-law analogues

slides.narration: Van’t Hoff noticed that osmotic pressure behaves just like gas pressure. At fixed temperature it is proportional to concentration; at fixed concentration it is proportional to absolute temperature; and solutions with equal molar concentrations at the same temperature have equal osmotic pressures. Combining these gives pi equals C R T, the same form as the ideal gas equation, which lets us find molar masses.

slides.heading: Worked example: molar mass of a protein
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** $1.5\ \text{g}$ of an enzyme is dissolved to make $100\ \text{mL}$ of solution at $310\ \text{K}$. The osmotic pressure is $6.43 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{bar}$. Find the molar mass ($R = 0.083\ \text{L bar K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$).

**Step 1.** $M_2 = \dfrac{w_2RT}{\pi V} = \dfrac{1.5 \times 0.083 \times 310}{6.43 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.100}$.

**Step 2.** Numerator $= 38.6$; denominator $= 6.43 \times 10^{-4}$.

**Step 3.** $M_2 \approx 6.0 \times 10^{4}\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

rows: Proteins and polymers are not damaged
Volume of solution is easy to measure

slides.narration: Rearrange pi equals C R T so that molar mass is the subject, keeping the volume in litres. The top of the fraction is about thirty eight point six, and the bottom is about six point four times ten to the minus four. The molar mass comes out near sixty thousand grams per mole. Osmotic pressure is ideal here: it works at room temperature and gives measurable values for such dilute solutions.

slides.heading: Isotonic, hypotonic and hypertonic solutions; reverse osmosis
slides.body_md: Solutions of equal osmotic pressure are **isotonic** (0.9% NaCl is isotonic with blood). A cell in a **hypertonic** solution loses water and shrinks (plasmolysis); in a **hypotonic** solution it gains water and swells or bursts. Applying a pressure **greater than** π to the solution forces solvent out through the membrane: **reverse osmosis**, used to desalinate sea water (cellulose acetate membranes).

slides.narration: Our red blood cells have the same osmotic pressure as saline of about nought point nine percent, so intravenous drips use that strength. In a stronger, hypertonic solution a cell loses water and shrinks; in a weaker, hypotonic one it takes in water and swells. If we push on sea water with more than its osmotic pressure, fresh water is forced out through a membrane: reverse osmosis, used in desalination plants and home water purifiers.

slides.body_md: Predict the direction of solvent flow or the fate of a cell in a solution.
slides.narration: Quick check. Solvent always flows through the membrane towards the more concentrated solution.

slides.heading: Quick check: van’t Hoff laws
slides.body_md: Use the van’t Hoff laws to compare osmotic pressures.
slides.narration: Quick check. Osmotic pressure is proportional to molar concentration and to absolute temperature.

slides.heading: Abnormal molar masses
slides.body_md: Colligative properties count particles. If a solute **dissociates** into ions, the observed effect is larger and the molar mass calculated is **lower** than the true value. If it **associates** (e.g. carboxylic acids dimerise in benzene), the effect is smaller and the calculated molar mass is **higher**.

visual.alt: Table of a dissociating and an associating solute and their effect on calculated molar mass

slides.narration: Sometimes the molar mass found from a colligative property does not match the formula. Potassium sulfate in water splits into three ions, so the effect is up to three times larger and the calculated molar mass comes out much too low. Benzoic acid in benzene pairs up into hydrogen-bonded dimers, so there are fewer particles and the molar mass appears too high. These are called abnormal molar masses.

slides.heading: The van’t Hoff factor
slides.body_md: The **van’t Hoff factor** $i$ corrects the equations. For dissociation of one formula unit into $n$ particles with degree $\alpha$, $i = 1 + (n-1)\alpha$; for association of $n$ molecules into one, $i = 1 - \alpha + \alpha/n$.

visual.alt: Table of the van’t Hoff factor and degree for dissociation and association

math: i = \frac{\text{observed colligative property}}{\text{calculated colligative property}} = \frac{\text{normal molar mass}}{\text{observed molar mass}}
\Delta T_\text{f} = iK_\text{f}m, \quad \Delta T_\text{b} = iK_\text{b}m, \quad \pi = iCRT, \quad \frac{\Delta p}{p^\circ} = i x_2
slides.narration: Van’t Hoff introduced a correction factor, i: the ratio of the observed colligative effect to the effect expected if the solute stayed as single molecules. It is greater than one for dissociation and less than one for association. Multiply each colligative equation by i. From i we can find the degree of dissociation or association using the formulas in the table.

slides.heading: Worked example: degree of dissociation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A $0.10\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$ aqueous solution of potassium sulfate freezes at $-0.43\ ^\circ\text{C}$. Calculate $i$ and the degree of dissociation. ($K_\text{f} = 1.86$)

**Step 1.** Calculated $\Delta T_\text{f} = 1.86 \times 0.10 = 0.186\ \text{K}$; observed $0.43\ \text{K}$.

**Step 2.** $i = 0.43 \div 0.186 = 2.31$.

**Step 3.** $n = 3$: $\alpha = (2.31 - 1) \div 2 = 0.655$, about $66\%$.

visual.alt: Table of the values in the potassium sulfate example

slides.narration: If potassium sulfate did not dissociate, the freezing point would drop by about nought point one nine kelvin. The observed drop is nought point four three, so i is about two point three. Each formula unit can give three ions, so alpha equals i minus one, divided by two: about nought point six six. Roughly two thirds of the salt is dissociated at this concentration.

slides.heading: Worked example: association of benzoic acid
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** $2.44\ \text{g}$ of benzoic acid ($M = 122$) in $50\ \text{g}$ of benzene lowers the freezing point by $1.12\ \text{K}$ ($K_\text{f} = 5.12$). Find $i$ and the percentage of acid that dimerises.

**Step 1.** Normal molality $= (2.44 \div 122) \div 0.050 = 0.40$; calculated $\Delta T_\text{f} = 5.12 \times 0.40 = 2.048\ \text{K}$.

**Step 2.** $i = 1.12 \div 2.048 = 0.547$.

**Step 3.** For dimers $i = 1 - \alpha/2$, so $\alpha = 2(1 - 0.547) = 0.906$: about $91\%$ dimerised.

visual.alt: Two benzoic acid molecules in equilibrium with one hydrogen-bonded dimer
visual.caption: In benzene, benzoic acid pairs up through two hydrogen bonds.

slides.narration: In benzene, benzoic acid molecules pair up through hydrogen bonds. Without pairing, the freezing point would fall by about two point zero five kelvin, but we observe only one point one two. So i is about nought point five five, less than one, as expected for association. For dimers i equals one minus half of alpha, giving alpha of about nought point nine one.

slides.heading: Quick check: van’t Hoff factor
slides.body_md: Decide whether i is above, below or equal to 1 for a solute.
slides.narration: Quick check. Does the solute split up, pair up, or stay as single molecules?

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Osmosis: solvent flow through a semipermeable membrane into the more concentrated solution.
van’t Hoff laws: π ∝ C, π ∝ T, equal π for equimolar solutions; π = CRT.
Osmotic pressure is best for molar masses of proteins and polymers.
Isotonic, hypertonic, hypotonic; reverse osmosis desalinates water.
Dissociation: i > 1, molar mass appears low; association: i < 1, appears high.

visual.alt: Summary table of colligative equations with the van’t Hoff factor

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Osmosis is the flow of solvent through a semipermeable membrane, and osmotic pressure obeys laws just like the gas laws, giving pi equals C R T. It is the best property for finding the molar masses of large molecules. Cells shrink in hypertonic solutions and swell in hypotonic ones. When solutes dissociate or associate, the van’t Hoff factor corrects every colligative equation.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Use V in litres, T in kelvin and R to match the pressure unit (0.083 L bar or 0.0821 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹).
Count ions: NaCl 2, CaCl₂ or K₂SO₄ 3, AlCl₃ or K₃[Fe(CN)₆] 4.
For association of carboxylic acids in benzene, n = 2.
State both reasons why osmotic pressure suits macromolecules.

visual.alt: Table of common traps in Part 2 and fixes

slides.narration: Final tips. In osmotic pressure problems use litres, kelvin and a gas constant that matches the pressure unit. Count ions carefully for salts and complexes. Carboxylic acids pair up in benzene, so n is two. And when asked why osmotic pressure suits proteins, give both reasons: room temperature and large measurable values.

sections.heading: 1. Colligative properties; relative lowering of vapour pressure
sections.body_md:
**Colligative properties** of dilute solutions of non-volatile solutes depend on the **number** of solute particles, not their nature: relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point and osmotic pressure.

**Relative lowering of vapour pressure** (from Raoult’s law, $p = p^\circ x_1$): $\dfrac{p^\circ - p}{p^\circ} = x_2$. For dilute solutions $x_2 \approx \dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \dfrac{w_2M_1}{M_2w_1}$, giving $M_2 = \dfrac{w_2M_1p^\circ}{w_1(p^\circ - p)}$.

The lowering of vapour pressure divided by the vapour pressure of the pure solvent; equal to the mole fraction of the solute.

sections.heading: 2. Elevation of boiling point
sections.body_md:
A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure; a solution’s vapour pressure is lower, so it boils at a higher temperature: $\Delta T_\text{b} = T_\text{b} - T^\circ_\text{b}$.

**Derivation:** near $T^\circ_\text{b}$ the vapour pressure curves of solvent and solution are nearly parallel straight lines, so $\Delta T_\text{b} \propto \Delta p$. With $p^\circ$ constant, $\Delta T_\text{b} \propto \Delta p/p^\circ = x_2 \approx n_2/n_1 = mM_1/1000$. Hence $\Delta T_\text{b} = K_\text{b}m$, with $K_\text{b}$ the **ebullioscopic (molal elevation) constant**, in K kg mol⁻¹ (water 0.52, benzene 2.53). Thermodynamically $K_\text{b} = \dfrac{R(T^\circ_\text{b})^2M_1}{1000\,\Delta_\text{vap}H}$.

Molar mass: $M_2 = \dfrac{1000K_\text{b}w_2}{\Delta T_\text{b}w_1}$.

key_terms.definition_md: The elevation of boiling point produced by a 1 mol kg⁻¹ solution; depends only on the solvent.

visual.alt: Vapour pressure against temperature near the boiling point: the solution curve runs just below and nearly parallel to the pure-solvent curve, so it reaches atmospheric pressure at a higher temperature; the gap between the two boiling points is the elevation
visual.caption: Illustrative; over this small range the curves are nearly straight and parallel, which is the basis of the derivation.

sections.heading: 3. Depression of freezing point
sections.body_md:
At the freezing point the solid and liquid solvent have equal vapour pressures. The solution’s vapour pressure is lower, so it equals that of the solid at a lower temperature: $\Delta T_\text{f} = T^\circ_\text{f} - T_\text{f}$.

**Derivation:** as for boiling point, $\Delta T_\text{f} \propto \Delta p \propto x_2 \propto m$, so $\Delta T_\text{f} = K_\text{f}m$, with $K_\text{f}$ the **cryoscopic (molal depression) constant** (water 1.86, benzene 5.12, camphor 37.7 K kg mol⁻¹); $K_\text{f} = \dfrac{R(T^\circ_\text{f})^2M_1}{1000\,\Delta_\text{fus}H}$.

Molar mass: $M_2 = \dfrac{1000K_\text{f}w_2}{\Delta T_\text{f}w_1}$. Uses: antifreeze, salting roads, camphor (Rast) method.

key_terms.definition_md: The depression of freezing point produced by a 1 mol kg⁻¹ solution; depends only on the solvent.

sections.heading: 4. Osmosis and osmotic pressure
sections.body_md:
**Diffusion:** spreading of particles from high to low concentration, no membrane. **Osmosis:** flow of solvent only through a **semipermeable membrane** (parchment, cellophane, copper ferrocyanide, animal bladder) from pure solvent or dilute solution into a more concentrated solution. **Osmotic pressure** $\pi$: the excess pressure on the solution that just stops osmosis.

**van’t Hoff laws:** Boyle–van’t Hoff ($\pi \propto C$ at constant $T$); Charles–van’t Hoff ($\pi \propto T$ at constant $C$); Avogadro–van’t Hoff (equimolar solutions at the same $T$ have equal $\pi$). Combined: $\pi = CRT$, $\pi V = nRT$, $M_2 = \dfrac{w_2RT}{\pi V}$ — best for proteins and polymers (room temperature, large values).

**Isotonic** solutions have equal $\pi$ (0.9% NaCl and blood); a cell **shrinks** in a hypertonic solution and **swells** in a hypotonic one. **Reverse osmosis:** pressure greater than $\pi$ forces solvent out of the solution; used for desalination of sea water.

key_terms.definition_md: A membrane that allows solvent molecules but not solute particles to pass.
The excess pressure that must be applied to a solution to prevent the flow of solvent into it through a semipermeable membrane.

sections.heading: 5. Abnormal molar masses and the van’t Hoff factor
sections.body_md:
Dissociation increases the number of particles (molar mass appears **low**); association decreases it (molar mass appears **high**, e.g. carboxylic acids dimerise in benzene).

$i = \dfrac{\text{observed colligative property}}{\text{calculated colligative property}} = \dfrac{\text{normal molar mass}}{\text{observed molar mass}}$.

Modified equations: $\Delta p/p^\circ = ix_2$; $\Delta T_\text{b} = iK_\text{b}m$; $\Delta T_\text{f} = iK_\text{f}m$; $\pi = iCRT$.
- **Dissociation** into $n$ ions: $i = 1 + (n-1)\alpha$, so $\alpha = \dfrac{i-1}{n-1}$.
- **Association** of $n$ molecules: $i = 1 - \alpha + \dfrac{\alpha}{n}$, so $\alpha = \dfrac{1-i}{1-1/n}$.

Fraction of the solute that dissociates into ions.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using the mass of solution instead of solvent for molality.
- Adding 273 to a temperature difference.
- Using mL instead of L, or a gas constant that does not match the pressure unit, in π = CRT.
- Forgetting the van’t Hoff factor for electrolytes, or using n = 2 for K₂SO₄ (it is 3).
- Mixing up hypotonic (cell swells) and hypertonic (cell shrinks).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Derivations (3 marks): the vapour pressure argument, the proportionality to x₂, and the final expression with the constant named.
- Numericals: formula, substitution with units, answer with units; full working is expected in ISC.
- van’t Hoff factor problems: calculated value, observed value, i, then α.

(a) What are colligative properties? Show that the relative lowering of vapour pressure of a solution of a non-volatile solute equals the mole fraction of the solute. [2]

(b) A solution contains 4.0% (by mass) of urea (M = 60) in water. Calculate the vapour pressure of this solution at 373 K, where pure water has a vapour pressure of 1.013 bar. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Properties of dilute solutions of non-volatile solutes that depend only on the number of solute particles. By Raoult’s law $p = p^\circ x_1 = p^\circ(1 - x_2)$, so $\dfrac{p^\circ - p}{p^\circ} = x_2$.

questions.stem_md: Calculate the boiling point of a solution of 18 g of glucose (M = 180) in 500 g of water at 1 atm. (Kb = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹; water boils at 373.15 K)

answer.model_answer_md: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure. The solution has a lower vapour pressure, so it boils at a higher temperature. Near the boiling point the vapour pressure–temperature curves of solvent and solution are almost parallel straight lines, so $\Delta T_\text{b} \propto \Delta p$. As $p^\circ$ is constant, $\Delta T_\text{b} \propto \Delta p/p^\circ = x_2$ (Raoult’s law). For a dilute solution $x_2 \approx n_2/n_1 = mM_1/1000$, so $\Delta T_\text{b} \propto m$, i.e. $\Delta T_\text{b} = K_\text{b}m$, where $K_\text{b}$, the ebullioscopic constant, depends only on the solvent.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The solution’s vapour pressure curve lies below that of the pure solvent, so it meets the line of atmospheric pressure at a higher temperature. Near $T_\text{b}^\circ$ the curves are nearly parallel straight lines, so $\Delta T_\text{b} \propto \Delta p$; with $p^\circ$ constant, $\Delta T_\text{b} \propto \Delta p/p^\circ = x_2 \approx n_2/n_1 = mM_1/1000$, giving $\Delta T_\text{b} = K_\text{b}m$.

(b) $M_2 = \dfrac{1000K_\text{b}w_2}{\Delta T_\text{b}w_1} = \dfrac{1000 \times 2.53 \times 2.5}{0.66 \times 75} = \dfrac{6325}{49.5} = 127.8\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: $0.90\ \text{g}$ of a non-electrolyte dissolved in $50\ \text{g}$ of water lowers the freezing point by $0.186\ \text{K}$. Calculate the molar mass of the solute. ($K_\text{f} = 1.86\ \text{K kg mol}^{-1}$)

questions.stem_md: Explain why spreading salt on icy roads melts the ice, and why calcium chloride is more effective than the same number of moles of sodium chloride.

answer.model_answer_md: Salt dissolves in the thin film of water on the ice, forming a solution whose freezing point is below 0 °C, so ice in contact with it melts. CaCl₂ gives three ions per formula unit (i = 3) while NaCl gives two, so it produces a larger depression of freezing point per mole.

questions.solution_md: Freezing point depression; more ions.

questions.stem_md: With the help of a vapour pressure–temperature diagram, explain why a solution freezes at a lower temperature than the pure solvent and derive ΔTf = Kf m.

answer.model_answer_md: At the freezing point the solid and liquid solvent have equal vapour pressures. A solution has a lower vapour pressure than the pure liquid, so its curve meets the steep solid-solvent curve at a lower temperature: the freezing point is depressed. Near $T^\circ_\text{f}$ the curves are nearly straight, so $\Delta T_\text{f} \propto \Delta p \propto \Delta p/p^\circ = x_2 \approx n_2/n_1 = mM_1/1000$. Hence $\Delta T_\text{f} = K_\text{f}m$, where $K_\text{f}$ is the cryoscopic constant of the solvent.

questions.solution_md: Equal vapour pressures; proportionality to m.

questions.stem_md: A transport company wants the radiator coolant of its trucks to stay liquid down to −5.58 °C. (a) What mass of ethylene glycol (M = 62) must be added to each 1.0 kg of water? (Kf = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹) (b) Why is ethylene glycol preferred to methanol for this purpose?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\Delta T_\text{f} = 5.58\ \text{K}$; $m = 5.58 \div 1.86 = 3.0\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$; mass $= 3.0 \times 62 = 186\ \text{g}$ per kg of water.

(b) Methanol is volatile and evaporates from a hot engine, while ethylene glycol is practically non-volatile (high boiling point), so it stays in the coolant and also raises its boiling point.

questions.solution_md: 186 g; glycol non-volatile.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain, using the vapour pressures of the solid and liquid solvent, why the freezing point of a solvent is lowered when a non-volatile solute is dissolved in it. [2]

(b) In the Rast method, 0.30 g of an organic compound is mixed with 15 g of camphor. The melting point of the mixture is 4.0 K lower than that of pure camphor (Kf = 37.7 K kg mol⁻¹). Calculate the molar mass of the compound, and state why camphor is chosen. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) At the freezing point the solid and the liquid solvent have the same vapour pressure. A dissolved solute lowers the vapour pressure of the liquid, so the solid and the solution reach equal vapour pressure only at a lower temperature.

(b) $M_2 = \dfrac{1000K_\text{f}w_2}{\Delta T_\text{f}w_1} = \dfrac{1000 \times 37.7 \times 0.30}{4.0 \times 15} = \dfrac{11310}{60} = 188.5\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. Camphor has a very large $K_\text{f}$, so even small amounts of solute give large, easily measured depressions.

questions.solution_md: Equal vapour pressures; 188.5 g/mol; large Kf.

questions.stem_md: Dry raisins left in water overnight swell up. This happens because:

sugar diffuses from the water into the raisins

applying a pressure smaller than its osmotic pressure to the sea-water side
heating the sea water above its boiling point
adding a solute to the fresh-water side

questions.stem_md: Calculate the osmotic pressure, in atm, of a $0.050\ \text{M}$ aqueous solution of sucrose at $27\ ^\circ\text{C}$. ($R = 0.0821\ \text{L atm K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$)

questions.stem_md: $5.0\ \text{g}$ of a synthetic polymer is dissolved to make $1.0\ \text{L}$ of solution at $300\ \text{K}$. Its osmotic pressure is $1.245 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{bar}$. What is the molar mass of the polymer, in g mol⁻¹? ($R = 0.083\ \text{L bar K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$)

A crystal of potassium permanganate slowly colours a beaker of water, while water passes through a parchment membrane into a sugar solution. Give two differences between these two processes, diffusion and osmosis.

answer.model_answer_md: Diffusion needs no membrane, while osmosis takes place through a semipermeable membrane. In diffusion solute (and solvent) particles move from higher to lower concentration, while in osmosis only solvent molecules move, from the dilute solution into the concentrated one; osmosis can be stopped by applying pressure, diffusion cannot.

questions.solution_md: Membrane; what moves.

questions.stem_md: Why must fluids given intravenously be isotonic with blood? What would happen to red blood cells placed in 0.5% (w/v) NaCl solution?

answer.model_answer_md: Isotonic fluids have the same osmotic pressure as blood, so there is no net flow of water into or out of the blood cells and they keep their shape. 0.5% NaCl is hypotonic (blood is isotonic with about 0.9%), so water enters the cells by osmosis and they swell and may burst.

questions.solution_md: No net flow; cells swell.

questions.stem_md: What is reverse osmosis? Give one practical use and state a property required of the membrane.

answer.model_answer_md: If a pressure greater than the osmotic pressure is applied to the solution side, solvent is forced out of the solution through the semipermeable membrane: reverse osmosis. It is used to desalinate sea water and in household water purifiers. The membrane must let water through but not dissolved ions, and withstand high pressure (e.g. cellulose acetate).

questions.solution_md: Definition; desalination; membrane.

questions.stem_md: State the Boyle–van’t Hoff, Charles–van’t Hoff and Avogadro–van’t Hoff laws for dilute solutions and show how they combine to give π = CRT.

answer.model_answer_md: Boyle–van’t Hoff: at constant temperature, osmotic pressure is proportional to molar concentration, $\pi \propto C$. Charles–van’t Hoff: at constant concentration, $\pi \propto T$. Avogadro–van’t Hoff: equimolar solutions at the same temperature have equal osmotic pressures, so the proportionality constant is the same for all solutes. Combining, $\pi \propto CT$, i.e. $\pi = CRT$, and since $C = n/V$, $\pi V = nRT$, where $R$ has the value of the gas constant.

questions.solution_md: Three laws; combination.

marking_scheme.step: Boyle–van’t Hoff and Charles–van’t Hoff laws

questions.stem_md: A solution of 0.60 g of a protein in 50 mL of water has an osmotic pressure of 3.32 × 10⁻³ bar at 300 K. (a) Calculate the molar mass of the protein (R = 0.083 L bar K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). (b) Why is osmotic pressure, rather than freezing point depression, used for this measurement?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $M_2 = \dfrac{w_2RT}{\pi V} = \dfrac{0.60 \times 0.083 \times 300}{3.32 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.050} = \dfrac{14.94}{1.66 \times 10^{-4}} = 90000\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

(b) It is measured at room temperature, so the protein is not denatured, and it gives measurable values even for very dilute solutions; the freezing point depression here would be far too small to measure.

questions.solution_md: 9.0 × 10⁴ g/mol; reasons.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define osmotic pressure. Why is it called a colligative property? [2]

(b) Calculate the osmotic pressure of a solution containing 1.8 g of glucose (M = 180) in 100 mL of solution at 27 °C (R = 0.0821 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). What concentration of NaCl, in g L⁻¹, would be isotonic with it at the same temperature, assuming complete dissociation? [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The excess pressure that must be applied to a solution to prevent the passage of pure solvent into it through a semipermeable membrane. It depends only on the molar concentration of solute particles ($\pi = CRT$), not on their nature.

(b) $C = (1.8 \div 180) \div 0.100 = 0.10\ \text{M}$; osmotic pressure $= 0.10 \times 0.0821 \times 300 = 2.46\ \text{atm}$. NaCl gives two ions, so it must be $0.050\ \text{M}$: $0.050 \times 58.5 = 2.93\ \text{g L}^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: Definition; 2.46 atm; 2.93 g/L NaCl.

questions.stem_md: A $0.20\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$ aqueous solution of barium chloride freezes at $-0.93\ ^\circ\text{C}$. Calculate the degree of dissociation of the salt. ($K_\text{f} = 1.86\ \text{K kg mol}^{-1}$)
The molar mass of sodium chloride (58.5) found from the freezing point of its dilute aqueous solution is close to 30. Explain, and calculate the van’t Hoff factor.

answer.model_answer_md: NaCl dissociates into Na⁺ and Cl⁻, almost doubling the number of particles, so the depression is about twice the expected value and the calculated molar mass about half the true value. i = normal ÷ observed molar mass = 58.5 ÷ 30 ≈ 1.95.

questions.solution_md: Dissociation; i ≈ 1.95.

questions.stem_md: 1.0 g of magnesium chloride (M = 95) is dissolved in 100 g of water. The solution freezes at −0.50 °C. Calculate (a) the van’t Hoff factor and (b) the degree of dissociation of the salt. (Kf = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹)

answer.model_answer_md:
Molality (no dissociation) $= (1.0 \div 95) \div 0.100 = 0.1053\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$; calculated $\Delta T_\text{f} = 1.86 \times 0.1053 = 0.196\ \text{K}$.

(a) $i = 0.50 \div 0.196 = 2.55$.

(b) $n = 3$: $\alpha = (2.55 - 1) \div 2 = 0.78$, about $78\%$.

questions.stem_md: 0.60 g of ethanoic acid (M = 60) in 25 g of benzene lowers the freezing point by 1.10 K (Kf = 5.12 K kg mol⁻¹). Calculate the van’t Hoff factor and the percentage of the acid that is dimerised.

answer.model_answer_md: Normal molality $= (0.60 \div 60) \div 0.025 = 0.40$; calculated $\Delta T_\text{f} = 5.12 \times 0.40 = 2.048\ \text{K}$. $i = 1.10 \div 2.048 = 0.537$. For dimers $i = 1 - \alpha/2$, so $\alpha = 2(1 - 0.537) = 0.926$: about $93\%$ dimerised.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the following aqueous solutions in order of increasing boiling point, giving reasons: 0.10 m glucose, 0.10 m NaCl, 0.10 m BaCl₂, 0.05 m AlCl₃. (Assume complete dissociation.)

answer.model_answer_md: ΔTb depends on i × m: glucose 1 × 0.10 = 0.10; NaCl 2 × 0.10 = 0.20; BaCl₂ 3 × 0.10 = 0.30; AlCl₃ 4 × 0.05 = 0.20. Increasing boiling point: glucose < NaCl = AlCl₃ < BaCl₂. The more solute particles per kg of water, the higher the boiling point.

questions.solution_md: Compare i × m.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define the van’t Hoff factor and write expressions for it in terms of the degree of dissociation and the degree of association. [2]

(b) A 0.10 mol kg⁻¹ aqueous solution of a weak monobasic acid HA freezes at −0.2046 °C. Calculate the degree of dissociation of the acid. (Kf = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹) [1½]

(c) Predict the freezing point of a 0.10 mol kg⁻¹ aqueous solution of K₄[Fe(CN)₆], assuming complete dissociation. [1½]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $i$ = observed colligative property ÷ calculated value (= normal molar mass ÷ observed molar mass). Dissociation into $n$ ions: $i = 1 + (n-1)\alpha$. Association of $n$ molecules: $i = 1 - \alpha + \alpha/n$.

(b) Calculated $\Delta T_\text{f} = 1.86 \times 0.10 = 0.186\ \text{K}$; $i = 0.2046 \div 0.186 = 1.10$; $\ce{HA <=> H+ + A-}$, $n = 2$: $\alpha = 1.10 - 1 = 0.10$ (10%).

(c) $\ce{K4[Fe(CN)6] -> 4K+ + Fe(CN)6^4-}$: $i = 5$; $\Delta T_\text{f} = 5 \times 1.86 \times 0.10 = 0.93\ \text{K}$; freezing point $-0.93\ ^\circ\text{C}$.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; α = 0.10; −0.93 °C.
